title: What Does It Mean to "Know Medicinal Chemistry"?
body_text: I thought this was an interesting and provocative article: “Who Knows Medicinal Chemistry?” The author (Daniele Andreotti) starts out with a statement that (to be honest) I have never heard before in my career: Most of us have heard some version of the sentence, and rather more of us than would admit have said it: “you do not really know medicinal chemistry - your job is to make the compounds”. It is seldom said unkindly; it arrives as a simple statement of fact, sorting people into those who design and those who execute. One reason I’ve never heard that one is that I came into the field as a PhD, and was thus expected to know (or learn!) medicinal chemistry, rather than just be the proverbial “pair of hands”. But a reason that I’ve never said it, either, is that I’ve spent my career in US labs rather than traditional European ones, where the split between “thinkers” and “doers” has long been more obvious. I remember people telling me back in the early 1990s that at the Swiss and German companies of the time that it could get to the point to where It Just Wasn’t Done for a PhD chemist to actually be standing in front of the fume hood doing chemistry - that was what your lab technicians were for, and that was, after all, what they were good at, since they had spent (and would spend) their entire careers there. In the US, new PhD chemists are indeed expected to do chemistry and to make molecules. And although some US research organizations have tried adopting this sort of organization, the split mentioned above usually works its way in over the years as people take on more managerial responsibilities - running a lab, running a group, running a section, running a department and so on. But even then you can hear them say that they miss being in the lab, or at least having the chance to do a little bench work. Working on budgets, staffing reports, performance reviews, and regulatory compliance issues does not always completely satisfy the soul, and that stuff can get a bit thick on the ground at times in middle-management. A personal aside: I knew very early on that I wanted to avoid that sort of thing, and as time went on I found that in addition I honestly did not enjoy telling other people what to do in the lab when I thought that they could have their own ideas about it. Most companies have either a formal or informal “scientific ladder” that roughly parallels the “managerial ladder”, and I have resolutely stayed on the former. Even now I have a fume hood and I use it with enjoyment! So I have never told anyone that they didn’t know - or didn’t have to know - med chem because they were just supposed to make molecules. In fact, I’m ready to talk people’s ears off about medicinal chemistry at whatever level they choose, and over the years I have cheerfully entertained questions about it not only from junior colleagues in the lab or from other departments, but from lab janitors and the dishwashing staff once they realize that I can be asked. No doubt some came to regret asking me in the first place, but that’s an occupational hazard. Andreotti’s piece is very much worth reading, because of insights like these: If the craft is learned largely through exposure to projects, then the person at the bench - synthesizing, watching the assay data come back, seeing which designs survived - is accumulating precisely the currency they are told they do not hold. To assign someone that work and then tell them they do not know medicinal chemistry is to withhold the education and then note the gap. The sentence may not describe a fixed difference in competence so much as help create one. dividing who is invited to reason from who is expected only to respond. There is a quieter point here, too. The difficulty of articulating why a design is right is easily read as a mark of sophistication; it can equally be a sign that the reasoning has never been fully unpacked, even to oneself. Expertise that cannot be transmitted is hard to distinguish, from the outside, from expertise that is not quite there - and putting an intuition into words is usually good for the intuition itself. That last part really resonates with me, because that’s one of the reasons I write this blog. For me, putting things into words is my way of thinking them out, and if I don’t find myself able to explain something that way then I have real doubts about whether I understand it. (That is also a very big reason why not one single word of what I post is done through the assistance of any AI system, nor ever will be). As Wittgenstein put it, “Anything that can be said can be said clearly”, although one has to note that (famously) he finished up his philosophy career by stating that in any language there are also things that simply cannot be said, dropping the microphone and getting off the stage after saying that “What we cannot speak of we must pass over in silence”. But I don’t think that we hit that limit much in this business! We have words to describe what we’re thinking about and what we’re trying to do, and if there aren’t good ones, we invent them and put them to use immediately. David Wootton, in his The Invention of Science, makes strong points about how no languages actually had the words for the concepts of experimental science and hypothesis testing. The very concepts barely existed, since various cultures saw such efforts as (for example) insults to the Gods, or sheer futility because obviously such questions were past human understanding, or affronts to the exalted masters of antiquity where all answers were to be found, etc. Andreotti also makes a very good point about how we assign expertise in this business, and how much of that might come down to luck: Grant, for a moment, that some people really do know more than others - as, plainly, they do. How do we tell? In practice we validate expertise largely by outcomes: a clinical candidate on the résumé, a program that advanced, a molecule that became a drug. The chemist with a candidate to their name is credited with knowing the field; the one without is quietly discounted. Yet in a discipline where the overwhelming majority of projects fail - for reasons no chemist controls, whether unexpected toxicity, an undruggable target, or biology that did not hold - outcomes are a noisy signal at best.2,3 A beautiful campaign can die because the hypothesis was wrong; a mediocre one can deliver a candidate because the target was forgiving. We have built a hierarchy of competence on a foundation dominated by attrition and luck, then treated the survivors as the arbiters of who understands the discipline - survivorship bias in a laboratory coat. Track record is not worthless; sustained success across diverse targets is informative. But a single candidate, or its absence, licenses less confidence about a person’s judgment than we habitually grant. The better definition of an expert medicinal chemist, the paper says, is not just what a person knows or what they’ve done, but what they can do with that knowledge, especially in the context of a research project. These are the people who can get their ideas across to biologists and toxicologists and managers from other parts of the organization, and put these ideas in a form where they can be clearly tested and improved. As we go more and more towards getting software and hardware assistance in this business, these skills will surely become even more important. Something to keep in mind!
